newsitem.title: UK: Thai white sugar premium could fall at end of crush.
newsitem.headline: Thai white sugar premium could fall at end of crush.

text.p: Thai white sugar premiums, inflated by strong Indonesian demand, could erode towards the end of cane crushing as mills start their re-melting programmes, analysts and brokers said on Thursday.
Cargoes of Thai 100 ICUMSA sugars were quoted at around $22 over London futures for March/April shipment, around $2/3 below the quote for 45 ICUMSA cargoes.
Traders said the strong prices were due to heavy buying from Indonesia, said to have imported as much as 1.3 million tonnes of whites, mainly from Thailand.
"The Thai white sugar premium is higher because there is not so much available," said one broker with a Japanese trade house.

"But the situation might change when we come to April because they will probably produce more white sugar if the white premium is attractive," he said, referring to the differential between London whites and New York raws.

Little extra production of white sugar was expected for the time being as this would reduce crushing capacity and millers preferred to maximise throughput at peak production time by turning out raws, he said.
Raw sugar premiums, in contrast, have slipped to around 20/25 points for March/May cargoes, down from the 35/40 points seen around a month ago.
Traders said while the low raws and high whites premia suggested Thai mills might be keen to pump out more white sugar, this was impeded by logistics.
"They have to get through all the cane and if they leave it too late, then the yields go right down and you have less sugar to start with," said one.
"They may just knock out the raws and then refine later on once they've finished the crush. They don't want it (cane) sitting on the ground."

When the re-melting starts, the quantity of whites to be produced will be largely a function of the world white/raw sugar differential. But the amount of cane to be available is also unclear as the crop started late.
The 1996/97 crushing season started in late November and is expected to last until May or early June.
Another factor is that at the end of the campaign Thai mills have to pay a premium for cane in order to maintain maximum factory capacity.
"At that time some of the mills do not want to pay the premium so they might change to production of white sugar," the broker said.
But the final split between white and raw sugar production will remain a guessing game for the moment.
Estimates among the London sugar trade for this year's Thai white sugar production ranged between 1.35 and 1.4 million tonnes tel quel.

"It's going to be a guess for some time because the main adjustment is an end-season activity. They started late...but that begs the question of how big the crop is," said Chris Pack, senior analyst at Czarnikow Sugar.
"The real bottle neck is how fast the growers can deliver to the factory," he said.
Although the differential is now widening, Thai millers are still likely to find the current level of around $72 unattractive after the $150 seen last April, even when the $22 local premium is added.
"Some people say the white sugar premium is attractive but compared with last year, it's not so much," the broker said.
"If the white sugar premium is $120, in that case they might consider (producing whites)," he added.
Thailand's total sugar production reached 2.85 million tonnes as it entered the 13th week of crushing with yields still trailing behind last season.
As of February 10, 29.08 million tonnes of cane was crushed by 46 mills to produce 1.73 million tonnes of raws and 1.12 million tonnes of whites.
